title: What is really happening to jobs? Separating AI hype from reality
content_html:
Publication

Key takeaways

  • AI’s effects on overall employment is likely small, though a tough job market for new graduates may be partly due to AI.
  • AI’s impact on worker productivity is mixed but generally positive.
  • Firm adoption has accelerated but unevenly across the economy.
  • Early evidence is hardly the last word on the future of work in an AI world.

Advances in AI models have sparked fears that rapid disruption of labor markets is imminent, if not already underway. A steady drumbeat of media articles has forecast a grim future for white-collar work due to AI.[1] Fears of an “AI jobs apocalypse” are often amplified by AI leaders themselves. For example, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, has predicted that AI could wipe out half of white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 20 percent. A labor market upheaval of this magnitude would cause enormous suffering for many households and pose a significant challenge for policymakers.

While the public has been debating AI’s potential impact on firms and their workers, research and data have been catching up. Our goal in this brief is to synthesize the fast-growing body of research on AI’s impact for policymakers and others eager to understand how AI is affecting the labor market right now. For ease of exposition, we organize this empirical evidence into a set of stylized facts, as follows:

  1. AI’s impact on aggregate employment is likely small right now.
  2. A tough market for recent graduates may be partly due to AI.
  3. AI’s impact on worker productivity is mixed but generally positive.
  4. Firm adoption has accelerated but unevenly across the economy.
  5. xEarly evidence is hardly the last word on AI’s impacts.

We will now explore each of these points in greater depth.

AI’s impact on labor market conditions is likely small right now.

No one can predict the future, but there is little evidence that AI is causing significant job losses right now. Unemployment among workers in occupations most exposed to AI-driven disruption is rising, but not faster than among those least exposed.[2] As shown in Figure 1, the unemployment rate for the top quintile of AI-exposed workers has risen by 0.77 percentage points since 2022, while the unemployment rate for the least-exposed workers rose slightly more, by 0.85 percentage points over the same period. These aggregate trends suggest a broadly softening labor market, rather than one characterized by AI-driven job losses.

Figure 1: Unemployment rate by AI-exposure quintile, 2015-2026 (quarterly)

There is also little evidence of AI depressing employment or job postings in the most highly exposed occupations. Employment trends in occupations with high exposure to AI are fairly stable.[4] While employment growth in coding-heavy occupations has slowed somewhat, it remains positive.[5] There is no evidence that AI adoption has negatively impacted firms’ job postings.[6] Indeed, online job postings for software developers — a very highly exposed occupation — have been growing faster than for other occupations over the last year.[7] Among firms that adopted enterprise AI, employment grew by 10 percent in the two years following adoption, an effect driven by firms with the highest per capita AI spending.[8]

What about the companies announcing layoffs, increasingly citing AI as a driving factor?[9] Both industry leaders and labor economists express some healthy skepticism about these claims.[10] While some narrow layoffs may be connected to AI-related automation, others appear driven by a desire to free up cash flow for AI investments or to reduce headcount after pandemic-era over-hiring. Human resource executives say the impacts of AI are more evident in role consolidation and hiring avoidance in roles where AI can automate many tasks.[11]

This doesn’t mean AI isn't having any negative impact on some workers; rather, the effects so far are more nuanced than an imminent “AI jobs apocalypse” would suggest. AI could be creating pockets of disruption that aren’t easily visible in aggregate economic data. In particular, there is some evidence that AI may be negatively affecting demand for young white-collar workers, as we discuss next.

A tough labor market for young workers may be partly due to AI

Recent graduates are facing the most challenging job market in years, with unemployment rates for new grads reaching 5.6 percent in early 2026, up 1.6 percentage points from three years earlier.[12] This rise has fueled concerns that AI is replacing many of the jobs recent graduates once sought. Junior roles often involve routine research, analysis, and writing tasks that can now largely be done with AI. Consistent with this intuition is empirical evidence that AI may be dampening demand for new hires.

In a widely discussed paper, Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen report a notable decline in employment among early-career workers in AI-exposed occupations, notably software developers and customer service representatives, since ChatGPT’s launch in 2022. As shown in Figure 2, by contrast, employment among older workers in those same occupations remained relatively stable or continued to grow. The authors liken these young workers to “canaries in the coal mine,” the first to experience labor market disruption from AI.[13] Other researchers have since identified similar negative effects on the hiring of young AI-exposed workers in the U.S. and the U.K., beginning in 2022.[14]

(a) Customer service representatives
(b) Software developers

The timing of this impact is somewhat surprising. AI model capabilities were very limited in 2022. Other factors may be at play, including rising interest rates, pandemic over-hiring, and remote work. For example, in response to rising inflation, the Federal Reserve aggressively hiked interest rates beginning in March 2022 — several months before ChatGPT’s public release the following November. Two new papers find that hiring in AI-exposed occupations began to decline after the Fed’s monetary policy shift but before ChatGPT’s debut.[15] Also, the rapid shift to remote work during the pandemic, which can slow on-the-job learning, erodes the value of hiring younger workers. New evidence suggests hiring in remote-friendly occupations began to skew toward more experienced workers after the pandemic.[16]

In response to concerns about these and other possible confounding effects, Brynjolfsson and coauthors added new controls. In these results, employment declines among entry-level workers are not notable until 2024.[17] It thus seems plausible that factors other than AI are driving declines in hiring young workers around 2022. However, by 2024, both AI adoption and model capabilities had advanced significantly, making the direct impacts of AI more plausible.

Hiring of entry-level workers in AI-exposed occupations clearly declined markedly around 2022. What is harder to determine is whether this decline constitutes clear evidence of AI’s impact on demand for young workers, now or in the future. Given other macroeconomic shocks to labor demand around this time, isolating AI’s impact is empirically challenging. This remains an open and active area of research.

The impact of AI on worker productivity is mixed but generally positive.

In experimental settings, generative AI tools — such as chatbots and coding tools — have often been found to disproportionately improve the performance of less experienced and poorer performing workers. In one such study, researchers analyzed the impact of a generative AI assistant on customer support agents in a large call center.[18] The assistant increased overall productivity by 15 percent, with gains highly concentrated among novice and less-skilled workers, who saw a 30 percent improvement in the number of issues resolved per hour. There was no performance improvement among highly skilled customer service agents, whose response quality fell slightly.

Other studies also show that AI tools generally speed up task completion, though the effects vary by task, context, and skill level. Figure 3 summarizes research findings on the impact of AI tools on speed across a variety of tasks. In software development, the use of GitHub Copilot — an AI tool that suggests code and functions — allowed tasks to be completed 56 percent faster, with gains concentrated among less-experienced programmers.[19] More modest impacts on software development were found in a separate paper, with effects ranging from 10 percent to 30 percent, depending on the firm where it was deployed.[20] In writing tasks, access to ChatGPT was found to reduce writing time for workers of all abilities and improve writing quality among low-ability writers.[21] Among young lawyers, the use of an AI tool was found to increase the speed of legal work, such as drafting contracts.[22] In medical settings, an assessment of AI scribes found some evidence that they increase the speed of medical note-taking, although the effects are small and occasional inaccuracies require physician oversight.[23]  

Figure 3: Experimental estimates of generative AI's effect on task speed

In many workplace settings, employees must determine when and how to deploy AI assistance, which complicates matters considerably. Dell’Acqua and coauthors document that AI’s capabilities are “jagged,” meaning performance can be strongly positive or negative depending on the specific task to which it is deployed.[24] Determining whether AI output is useful or needs further refinement can require skilled judgment. For example, when researchers deployed an AI assistant to help Kenyan entrepreneurs, less-skilled entrepreneurs posted lower revenues and profits from using an AI tool than those who grew their businesses without it.[25] Examining why, the researchers found that less-skilled entrepreneurs were more likely to act on generic advice from the AI tool that was detrimental to their specific situations, while better performers extracted suggestions more tailored to their business needs.

While AI can make some employees more individually productive, it can also narrow the range of creative ideas. The use of AI in creative writing tasks was found to increase the quality of stories produced by less-skilled writers, but AI-generated stories were much more similar to one another than human-generated ones.[26] Hao and coauthors found that, while scientists who adopt AI tools publish more papers, AI adoption reduces the total number of topics studied and scientists’ engagement with one another.[27]

AI clearly has the potential to improve worker performance across many settings. However, several frictions could prevent the gains observed in experimental studies from showing up in aggregate productivity measures yet. The share of tasks that AI can profitably speed up may be small relative to the total number of economic tasks.[28] Bottlenecks in processes where AI cannot currently assist could limit productivity gains for a time.[29] Also, when firms adopt new technologies, measured productivity can initially fall because firms need to divert resources to reorganize functions and make complementary investments.[30] While AI is likely to boost productivity eventually, given the current pace of firm adoption, it may not be visible in aggregate statistics yet.

Firm adoption has accelerated but unevenly across the economy.

If AI is truly a transformative technology, whether its sweeping effects occur over three years or 20 years fundamentally changes the policy problem. A swift transformation could displace many workers at once, while a slower one gives policymakers and workers more time to adapt. One of the most important indicators of the timing and distribution of AI’s potential economy-wide effects is the pace of firm adoption.

Figure 4: AI adoption at work, 2023-2026

Surveys of firms show a wide range of adoption rates, but all show rapid growth in the use of AI. Figure 4 shows several widely cited measures of firm adoption. The most conservative estimate of firm adoption is the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), a nationally representative survey of businesses, which currently estimates that about 20 percent of firms use AI. Other measures of AI use in the workplace generally show higher rates of firm adoption; at the high end, a survey of executives in U.S. firms found that over 80 percent of employees use AI at work.[31] Ramp, a fintech expense management company, estimates that over 50 percent of its clients are spending money on AI tools and AI vendors. A nationally representative survey of households finds that over 40 percent of employed respondents use AI at work.

Variance in adoption rates across measures is largely due to differences in methodology and sample composition. Larger firms are more likely to adopt AI, so employment-weighted adoption rates are higher than simple firm counts would suggest. Ramp clearly states in the methodology for its AI index that firms using its platform are not a representative sample of businesses and are skewed toward technology firms, which have higher rates of AI adoption. In a review of the surveys on AI adoption, a recent Federal Reserve research report noted good reasons to favor the relatively low Census estimates, which use a national sampling frame, and showed how differences in adoption rates across surveys narrow considerably when each is weighted by employment.[32] 

The distribution of firms that are adopting AI tells us where AI’s effects will likely happen first. Currently, the survey evidence suggests AI adoption is concentrated among technology firms and information-intensive sectors like finance. The most common AI deployments are in sales and marketing, IT, strategy, finance, and accounting. Even among adopters, AI use remains narrow rather than broad, limited either to one or two business functions or to low-frequency use across a broader set of tasks, with comprehensive AI integration the exception rather than the rule.[33] A recent McKinsey survey found that most businesses remain in the experimentation and piloting phase of AI, with only a few large companies leading the way in scaling beyond pilots. [34]

AI adoption also appears to have had little effect on employment. In the Census data, only 5 percent of firms report any employment impact, with equal numbers reporting gains and losses. Eighty percent of executives surveyed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta said AI investments have yet to alter their headcount or improve productivity. A large-scale Danish study linking data on AI adoption by workers to firms found that AI adoption results in the restructuring of worker tasks and time, but that these changes are not yet affecting worker employment, hours or earnings.[35] A recent study found that among firms adopting AI, employment grew by 10 percent in the two years following adoption.[36]

Taken together, the data suggest firm AI adoption is moving quickly but unevenly throughout the economy, with many firms still in the experimentation stage and only the more advanced adopters deploying AI more broadly.

Conclusion: Existing evidence is hardly the last word.

Technological advances typically take years, even decades, to transform businesses and labor markets. In 1987, economist Robert Solow famously quipped, “You can see the computer age everywhere but the productivity statistics.” This lag between innovation and growth occurs because firms' adoption of new technologies is often uneven and slow. Firms, for instance, invested heavily in PC technology in the 1980s. But leveraging the advantages of the PC required additional investments — in enterprise software, worker retraining, and organizational restructuring. These adoption frictions were a major reason measurable economic returns from the computer revolution did not appear until the late 1990s.

It is always difficult to predict what will come next. In Silicon Valley, opinion is sharply divided between those who see AI as a “normal technology” — transformative but gradual, akin to past technologies — and those who predict world-altering effects as early as 2027. The strongest case for AI as a normal technology is history. Previous technological revolutions have eliminated or reduced labor demand in some occupations while simultaneously creating new jobs and industries. As a result, aggregate employment increased, even as the nature of work and the economy changed.

In contrast, those who believe that AI is fundamentally different point to the uniquely fast pace of AI adoption, AI’s disproportionate impact on cognitive work, and the cross-cutting nature of AI, threatening not just one occupation but much white-collar work. Regardless of which camp is correct, technological revolutions can be deeply disruptive to individuals, making it crucial to better understand — as quickly as possible — AI's evolving impact on the labor market and prepare potential policy responses.

About the Authors

Neale Mahoney is the Trione Director of SIEPR and the TG Wijaya Professor of Economics at Stanford University. He previously served as a Special Policy Advisor in the White House National Economic Council.

Erika McEntarfer is a Research Scholar and Distinguished Policy Fellow at SIEPR. She served as Commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics until August 2025 and, before that, was a Senior Economist in the White House Council of Economic Advisers.

Karsen Wahal is a researcher at SIEPR. He recently graduated from Stanford with a B.A. (with honors) in economics, a B.S. in mathematics and an M.S. in computer science. His primary research interests are in the economics of AI, particularly through the lenses of labor economics, economic growth, market design, and political economy.

The Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR) catalyzes and promotes evidence-based knowledge about pressing economic issues, leading to better-informed policy solutions for generations to come. We are a nonpartisan research institute, and SIEPR policy briefs reflect the views and ideas of the authors only.

In software development, the use of GitHub Copilot — an AI tool that suggests code and functions — allowed tasks to be completed 56 percent faster, with gains concentrated among less-experienced programmers.[19] More modest impacts on software development were found in a separate paper, with effects ranging from 10 percent to 30 percent, depending on the firm where it was deployed.[20] In writing tasks, access to ChatGPT was found to reduce writing time for workers of all abilities and improve writing quality among low-ability writers.[21] Among young lawyers, the use of an AI tool was found to increase the speed of legal work, such as drafting contracts.[22] In medical settings, an assessment of AI scribes found some evidence that they increase the speed of medical note-taking, although the effects are small and occasional inaccuracies require physician oversight.[23] Figure 3: Experimental estimates of generative AI's effect on task speed Source: Authors' compilation of randomized and field experiments. Note: Each point is the estimated effect of giving workers access to generative AI on the time taken to complete representative tasks, colored by the AI model generation used. Choi et al. (2023) is shown as a range (the span across tasks). Cui et al. (2025) and Brynjolfsson et al. (2023) are converted from output-per-hour measures, and Brynjolfsson et al. is a staggered-rollout, quasi-experiment rather than a randomized trial. Estimates are task-level and short-horizon, and tasks differ across studies, so magnitudes are not strictly comparable. In many workplace settings, employees must determine when and how to deploy AI assistance, which complicates matters considerably. Dell’Acqua and coauthors document that AI’s capabilities are “jagged,” meaning performance can be strongly positive or negative depending on the specific task to which it is deployed.[24] Determining whether AI output is useful or needs further refinement can require skilled judgment. For example, when researchers deployed an AI assistant to help Kenyan entrepreneurs, less-skilled entrepreneurs posted lower revenues and profits from using an AI tool than those who grew their businesses without it.[25] Examining why, the researchers found that less-skilled entrepreneurs were more likely to act on generic advice from the AI tool that was detrimental to their specific situations, while better performers extracted suggestions more tailored to their business needs.While AI can make some employees more individually productive, it can also narrow the range of creative ideas. The use of AI in creative writing tasks was found to increase the quality of stories produced by less-skilled writers, but AI-generated stories were much more similar to one another than human-generated ones.[26] Hao and coauthors found that, while scientists who adopt AI tools publish more papers, AI adoption reduces the total number of topics studied and scientists’ engagement with one another.[27]AI clearly has the potential to improve worker performance across many settings. However, several frictions could prevent the gains observed in experimental studies from showing up in aggregate productivity measures yet. The share of tasks that AI can profitably speed up may be small relative to the total number of economic tasks.[28] Bottlenecks in processes where AI cannot currently assist could limit productivity gains for a time.[29] Also, when firms adopt new technologies, measured productivity can initially fall because firms need to divert resources to reorganize functions and make complementary investments.[30] While AI is likely to boost productivity eventually, given the current pace of firm adoption, it may not be visible in aggregate statistics yet.Firm adoption has accelerated but unevenly across the economy.If AI is truly a transformative technology, whether its sweeping effects occur over three years or 20 years fundamentally changes the policy problem. A swift transformation could displace many workers at once, while a slower one gives policymakers and workers more time to adapt. One of the most important indicators of the timing and distribution of AI’s potential economy-wide effects is the pace of firm adoption.Figure 4: AI adoption at work, 2023-2026 Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS); Stanford Digital Economy Lab/Real-Time Population Survey (Bick, Blandin & Deming, 2024); Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Survey of Business Uncertainty; Ramp AI index. The Census revised the BTOS instrument in November 2025 to ask firms about all AI use at the firm; previously, the survey asked whether AI was used ‘to produce goods and services’. Note: Series are not directly comparable. BTOS = unweighted share of firms using AI (biweekly; the break marks the November 2025 change in question wording). Bick, Blandin, and Deming = the share of individuals using generative AI at work. Survey of Business Uncertainty = employment-weighted share of firms using any AI. Ramp = the share of businesses on its platform (not a representative sample) purchasing AI services. Surveys of firms show a wide range of adoption rates, but all show rapid growth in the use of AI. Figure 4 shows several widely cited measures of firm adoption. The most conservative estimate of firm adoption is the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), a nationally representative survey of businesses, which currently estimates that about 20 percent of firms use AI. Other measures of AI use in the workplace generally show higher rates of firm adoption; at the high end, a survey of executives in U.S. firms found that over 80 percent of employees use AI at work.[31] Ramp, a fintech expense management company, estimates that over 50 percent of its clients are spending money on AI tools and AI vendors. A nationally representative survey of households finds that over 40 percent of employed respondents use AI at work.Variance in adoption rates across measures is largely due to differences in methodology and sample composition. Larger firms are more likely to adopt AI, so employment-weighted adoption rates are higher than simple firm counts would suggest. Ramp clearly states in the methodology for its AI index that firms using its platform are not a representative sample of businesses and are skewed toward technology firms, which have higher rates of AI adoption. In a review of the surveys on AI adoption, a recent Federal Reserve research report noted good reasons to favor the relatively low Census estimates, which use a national sampling frame, and showed how differences in adoption rates across surveys narrow considerably when each is weighted by employment.[32] The distribution of firms that are adopting AI tells us where AI’s effects will likely happen first. Currently, the survey evidence suggests AI adoption is concentrated among technology firms and information-intensive sectors like finance. The most common AI deployments are in sales and marketing, IT, strategy, finance, and accounting. Even among adopters, AI use remains narrow rather than broad, limited either to one or two business functions or to low-frequency use across a broader set of tasks, with comprehensive AI integration the exception rather than the rule.[33] A recent McKinsey survey found that most businesses remain in the experimentation and piloting phase of AI, with only a few large companies leading the way in scaling beyond pilots. [34]AI adoption also appears to have had little effect on employment. In the Census data, only 5 percent of firms report any employment impact, with equal numbers reporting gains and losses. Eighty percent of executives surveyed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta said AI investments have yet to alter their headcount or improve productivity. A large-scale Danish study linking data on AI adoption by workers to firms found that AI adoption results in the restructuring of worker tasks and time, but that these changes are not yet affecting worker employment, hours or earnings.[35] A recent study found that among firms adopting AI, employment grew by 10 percent in the two years following adoption.[36]Taken together, the data suggest firm AI adoption is moving quickly but unevenly throughout the economy, with many firms still in the experimentation stage and only the more advanced adopters deploying AI more broadly.Conclusion: Existing evidence is hardly the last word.Technological advances typically take years, even decades, to transform businesses and labor markets. In 1987, economist Robert Solow famously quipped, “You can see the computer age everywhere but the productivity statistics.” This lag between innovation and growth occurs because firms' adoption of new technologies is often uneven and slow. Firms, for instance, invested heavily in PC technology in the 1980s. But leveraging the advantages of the PC required additional investments — in enterprise software, worker retraining, and organizational restructuring. These adoption frictions were a major reason measurable economic returns from the computer revolution did not appear until the late 1990s.It is always difficult to predict what will come next. In Silicon Valley, opinion is sharply divided between those who see AI as a “normal technology” — transformative but gradual, akin to past technologies — and those who predict world-altering effects as early as 2027. The strongest case for AI as a normal technology is history. Previous technological revolutions have eliminated or reduced labor demand in some occupations while simultaneously creating new jobs and industries. As a result, aggregate employment increased, even as the nature of work and the economy changed.In contrast, those who believe that AI is fundamentally different point to the uniquely fast pace of AI adoption, AI’s disproportionate impact on cognitive work, and the cross-cutting nature of AI, threatening not just one occupation but much white-collar work. Regardless of which camp is correct, technological revolutions can be deeply disruptive to individuals, making it crucial to better understand — as quickly as possible — AI's evolving impact on the labor market and prepare potential policy responses. blocks.html_en: No one can predict the future, but there is little evidence that AI is causing significant job losses right now. Unemployment among workers in occupations most exposed to AI-driven disruption is rising, but not faster than among those least exposed.[2] As shown in Figure 1, the unemployment rate for the top quintile of AI-exposed workers has risen by 0.77 percentage points since 2022, while the unemployment rate for the least-exposed workers rose slightly more, by 0.85 percentage points over the same period. These aggregate trends suggest a broadly softening labor market, rather than one characterized by AI-driven job losses.

blocks.html_en: What about the companies announcing layoffs, increasingly citing AI as a driving factor?[9] Both industry leaders and labor economists express some healthy skepticism about these claims.[10] While some narrow layoffs may be connected to AI-related automation, others appear driven by a desire to free up cash flow for AI investments or to reduce headcount after pandemic-era over-hiring. Human resource executives say the impacts of AI are more evident in role consolidation and hiring avoidance in roles where AI can automate many tasks.[11]

blocks.html_en: Recent graduates are facing the most challenging job market in years, with unemployment rates for new grads reaching 5.6 percent in early 2026, up 1.6 percentage points from three years earlier.[12] This rise has fueled concerns that AI is replacing many of the jobs recent graduates once sought. blocks.html_en: The timing of this impact is somewhat surprising. AI model capabilities were very limited in 2022. Other factors may be at play, including rising interest rates, pandemic over-hiring, and remote work. For example, in response to rising inflation, the Federal Reserve aggressively hiked interest rates beginning in March 2022 — several months before ChatGPT’s public release the following November. Two new papers find that hiring in AI-exposed occupations began to decline after the Fed’s monetary policy shift but before ChatGPT’s debut.[15] Also, the rapid shift to remote work during the pandemic, which can slow on-the-job learning, erodes the value of hiring younger workers. New evidence suggests hiring in remote-friendly occupations began to skew toward more experienced workers after the pandemic.[16]

blocks.html_en: In experimental settings, generative AI tools — such as chatbots and coding tools — have often been found to disproportionately improve the performance of less experienced and poorer performing workers. In one such study, researchers analyzed the impact of a generative AI assistant on customer support agents in a large call center.[18] The assistant increased overall productivity by 15 percent, with gains highly concentrated among novice and less-skilled workers, who saw a 30 percent improvement in the number of issues resolved per hour. There was no performance improvement among highly skilled customer service agents, whose response quality fell slightly.

blocks.html_en: Other studies also show that AI tools generally speed up task completion, though the effects vary by task, context, and skill level. Figure 3 summarizes research findings on the impact of AI tools on speed across a variety of tasks. In software development, the use of GitHub Copilot — an AI tool that suggests code and functions — allowed tasks to be completed 56 percent faster, with gains concentrated among less-experienced programmers.[19] More modest impacts on software development were found in a separate paper, with effects ranging from 10 percent to 30 percent, depending on the firm where it was deployed.[20] In writing tasks, access to ChatGPT was found to reduce writing time for workers of all abilities and improve writing quality among low-ability writers.[21] Among young lawyers, the use of an AI tool was found to increase the speed of legal work, such as drafting contracts.[22] In medical settings, an assessment of AI scribes found some evidence that they increase the speed of medical note-taking, although the effects are small and occasional inaccuracies require physician oversight.[23]

blocks.html_en: In many workplace settings, employees must determine when and how to deploy AI assistance, which complicates matters considerably. Dell’Acqua and coauthors document that AI’s capabilities are “jagged,” meaning performance can be strongly positive or negative depending on the specific task to which it is deployed.[24] Determining whether AI output is useful or needs further refinement can require skilled judgment. For example, when researchers deployed an AI assistant to help Kenyan entrepreneurs, less-skilled entrepreneurs posted lower revenues and profits from using an AI tool than those who grew their businesses without it.[25] Examining why, the researchers found that less-skilled entrepreneurs were more likely to act on generic advice from the AI tool that was detrimental to their specific situations, while better performers extracted suggestions more tailored to their business needs.

blocks.html_en: AI clearly has the potential to improve worker performance across many settings. However, several frictions could prevent the gains observed in experimental studies from showing up in aggregate productivity measures yet. The share of tasks that AI can profitably speed up may be small relative to the total number of economic tasks.[28] Bottlenecks in processes where AI cannot currently assist could limit productivity gains for a time.[29] Also, when firms adopt new technologies, measured productivity can initially fall because firms need to divert resources to reorganize functions and make complementary investments.[30] While AI is likely to boost productivity eventually, given the current pace of firm adoption, it may not be visible in aggregate statistics yet.

sentences.en: AI clearly has the potential to improve worker performance across many settings.
sentences.zh: 人工智能显然有潜力在许多环境中提高员工的绩效。

sentences.en: However, several frictions could prevent the gains observed in experimental studies from showing up in aggregate productivity measures yet.
sentences.zh: 然而，一些摩擦可能会阻止实验研究中观察到的成果在总体生产率指标中体现出来。

sentences.en: The share of tasks that AI can profitably speed up may be small relative to the total number of economic tasks.[28] Bottlenecks in processes where AI cannot currently assist could limit productivity gains for a time.[29] Also, when firms adopt new technologies, measured productivity can initially fall because firms need to divert resources to reorganize functions and make complementary investments.[30] While AI is likely to boost productivity eventually, given the current pace of firm adoption, it may not be visible in aggregate statistics yet.
sentences.zh: 相对于经济任务的总数，人工智能可以有利地加速的任务份额可能很小。 [28]人工智能目前无法提供帮助的流程中的瓶颈可能会暂时限制生产力的提高。 [29]此外，当企业采用新技术时，衡量的生产率最初可能会下降，因为企业需要转移资源来重组职能并进行补充投资。 [30]虽然人工智能最终可能会提高生产力，但考虑到目前企业采用的速度，它可能在总体统计数据中还无法显现出来。

blocks.html_en: Firm adoption has accelerated but unevenly across the economy.

sentences.en: Firm adoption has accelerated but unevenly across the economy.
sentences.zh: 企业的采用速度有所加快，但在整个经济中并不均衡。

blocks.html_en: If AI is truly a transformative technology, whether its sweeping effects occur over three years or 20 years fundamentally changes the policy problem. A swift transformation could displace many workers at once, while a slower one gives policymakers and workers more time to adapt. One of the most important indicators of the timing and distribution of AI’s potential economy-wide effects is the pace of firm adoption.

sentences.en: A swift transformation could displace many workers at once, while a slower one gives policymakers and workers more time to adapt.
sentences.zh: 快速的转型可能会立即取代许多工人，而较慢的转型则可以给政策制定者和工人更多的时间来适应。

sentences.en: One of the most important indicators of the timing and distribution of AI’s potential economy-wide effects is the pace of firm adoption.
sentences.zh: 人工智能对整个经济产生潜在影响的时间和分布的最重要指标之一是企业采用的速度。

blocks.html_en: Surveys of firms show a wide range of adoption rates, but all show rapid growth in the use of AI. Figure 4 shows several widely cited measures of firm adoption. The most conservative estimate of firm adoption is the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), a nationally representative survey of businesses, which currently estimates that about 20 percent of firms use AI. Other measures of AI use in the workplace generally show higher rates of firm adoption; at the high end, a survey of executives in U.S. firms found that over 80 percent of employees use AI at work.[31] Ramp, a fintech expense management company, estimates that over 50 percent of its clients are spending money on AI tools and AI vendors. A nationally representative survey of households finds that over 40 percent of employed respondents use AI at work.

sentences.en: Surveys of firms show a wide range of adoption rates, but all show rapid growth in the use of AI.
sentences.zh: 对企业的调查显示，采用率存在很大差异，但都显示人工智能的使用在快速增长。

sentences.zh: 一项全国范围内的家庭代表性调查发现，超过 40% 的就业受访者在工作中使用人工智能。

blocks.html_en: Variance in adoption rates across measures is largely due to differences in methodology and sample composition. Larger firms are more likely to adopt AI, so employment-weighted adoption rates are higher than simple firm counts would suggest. Ramp clearly states in the methodology for its AI index that firms using its platform are not a representative sample of businesses and are skewed toward technology firms, which have higher rates of AI adoption. In a review of the surveys on AI adoption, a recent Federal Reserve research report noted good reasons to favor the relatively low Census estimates, which use a national sampling frame, and showed how differences in adoption rates across surveys narrow considerably when each is weighted by employment.[32]

sentences.en: Larger firms are more likely to adopt AI, so employment-weighted adoption rates are higher than simple firm counts would suggest.
sentences.zh: 较大的公司更有可能采用人工智能，因此就业加权采用率高于简单的公司计数所显示的水平。

sentences.en: In a review of the surveys on AI adoption, a recent Federal Reserve research report noted good reasons to favor the relatively low Census estimates, which use a national sampling frame, and showed how differences in adoption rates across surveys narrow considerably when each is weighted by employment.[32]
sentences.zh: 在对人工智能采用率调查的回顾中，美联储最近的一份研究报告指出了支持相对较低的人口普查估计值的充分理由，该估计值使用了全国抽样框架，并显示了当每项调查都按就业加权时，不同调查的采用率差异如何大幅缩小。 [32]

blocks.html_en: The distribution of firms that are adopting AI tells us where AI’s effects will likely happen first. Currently, the survey evidence suggests AI adoption is concentrated among technology firms and information-intensive sectors like finance. The most common AI deployments are in sales and marketing, IT, strategy, finance, and accounting. Even among adopters, AI use remains narrow rather than broad, limited either to one or two business functions or to low-frequency use across a broader set of tasks, with comprehensive AI integration the exception rather than the rule.[33] A recent McKinsey survey found that most businesses remain in the experimentation and piloting phase of AI, with only a few large companies leading the way in scaling beyond pilots. [34]

blocks.html_en: AI adoption also appears to have had little effect on employment. In the Census data, only 5 percent of firms report any employment impact, with equal numbers reporting gains and losses. Eighty percent of executives surveyed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta said AI investments have yet to alter their headcount or improve productivity. A large-scale Danish study linking data on AI adoption by workers to firms found that AI adoption results in the restructuring of worker tasks and time, but that these changes are not yet affecting worker employment, hours or earnings.[35] A recent study found that among firms adopting AI, employment grew by 10 percent in the two years following adoption.[36]

blocks.html_en: Taken together, the data suggest firm AI adoption is moving quickly but unevenly throughout the economy, with many firms still in the experimentation stage and only the more advanced adopters deploying AI more broadly.

sentences.en: Taken together, the data suggest firm AI adoption is moving quickly but unevenly throughout the economy, with many firms still in the experimentation stage and only the more advanced adopters deploying AI more broadly.
sentences.zh: 总而言之，这些数据表明，企业人工智能的采用正在迅速发展，但在整个经济中并不均衡，许多企业仍处于实验阶段，只有更先进的采用者才能更广泛地部署人工智能。

blocks.html_en: Conclusion: Existing evidence is hardly the last word.

blocks.html_en: Technological advances typically take years, even decades, to transform businesses and labor markets. In 1987, economist Robert Solow famously quipped, “You can see the computer age everywhere but the productivity statistics.” This lag between innovation and growth occurs because firms' adoption of new technologies is often uneven and slow. Firms, for instance, invested heavily in PC technology in the 1980s. But leveraging the advantages of the PC required additional investments — in enterprise software, worker retraining, and organizational restructuring. These adoption frictions were a major reason measurable economic returns from the computer revolution did not appear until the late 1990s.

blocks.html_en: It is always difficult to predict what will come next. In Silicon Valley, opinion is sharply divided between those who see AI as a “normal technology” — transformative but gradual, akin to past technologies — and those who predict world-altering effects as early as 2027. The strongest case for AI as a normal technology is history. Previous technological revolutions have eliminated or reduced labor demand in some occupations while simultaneously creating new jobs and industries. As a result, aggregate employment increased, even as the nature of work and the economy changed.

blocks.html_en: In contrast, those who believe that AI is fundamentally different point to the uniquely fast pace of AI adoption, AI’s disproportionate impact on cognitive work, and the cross-cutting nature of AI, threatening not just one occupation but much white-collar work. Regardless of which camp is correct, technological revolutions can be deeply disruptive to individuals, making it crucial to better understand — as quickly as possible — AI's evolving impact on the labor market and prepare potential policy responses.

要点

  • 人工智能对整体就业的影响可能很小，尽管应届毕业生就业市场的艰难可能部分归因于人工智能。
  • 人工智能对员工生产力的影响有好有坏，但总体来说是积极的。
  • 企业的采用速度有所加快，但在整个经济中并不均衡。
  • 早期证据并不是人工智能世界未来工作的最终定论。

人工智能模型的进步引发了人们的担忧，即劳动力市场的快速混乱即使尚未发生，也即将发生。 媒体文章的不断报道预测，人工智能将给白领工作带来严峻的未来。[1]人工智能领导者本身往往会放大对“人工智能就业灾难”的担忧。 例如，Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 预测，人工智能可能会消灭一半的白领工作，并将失业率推至 20%。 如此大规模的劳动力市场动荡将给许多家庭带来巨大痛苦，并对政策制定者构成重大挑战。

尽管公众一直在争论人工智能对企业及其员工的潜在影响，但研究和数据已经迎头赶上。 我们本简报的目标是综合关于人工智能对政策制定者和其他渴望了解人工智能目前如何影响劳动力市场的人的影响的快速增长的研究。 为了便于说明，我们将这些经验证据组织成一组程式化的事实，如下：

  1. 目前人工智能对总体就业的影响可能很小。
  2. 对于应届毕业生来说，市场的艰难可能部分是由于人工智能。
  3. 人工智能对员工生产力的影响有好有坏，但总体来说是积极的。
  4. 企业的采用速度有所加快，但在整个经济中并不均衡。
  5. x早期证据并不是人工智能影响的最终定论。

我们现在将更深入地探讨每一点。

目前人工智能对劳动力市场状况的影响可能很小。

没有人能够预测未来，但几乎没有证据表明人工智能目前正在造成大量失业。 受人工智能驱动的破坏最严重的职业中工人的失业率正在上升，但并不比那些受人工智能影响最小的职业的工人失业率上升。 [2]如图 1 所示，自 2022 年以来，受人工智能影响最大的五分之一工人的失业率上升了 0.77 个百分点，而受人工智能影响最小的工人的失业率略有上升，同期上升了 0.85 个百分点。 这些总体趋势表明劳动力市场普遍疲软，而不是人工智能驱动的失业市场。

图 1：2015 年至 2026 年按人工智能五分位数划分的失业率（季度）

几乎没有证据表明人工智能会抑制高风险职业的就业或职位发布。 与人工智能接触程度较高的职业的就业趋势相当稳定。[4]虽然编码密集型职业的就业增长有所放缓，但仍保持积极态势。[5]没有证据表明人工智能的采用对公司的职位发布产生了负面影响。[6]事实上，软件开发人员的在线招聘信息（一种曝光率非常高的职业）在过去的一年里比其他职业的增长速度更快。 [7]在采用企业人工智能的公司中，就业率在采用后的两年内增长了 10%，这是由人均人工智能支出最高的公司推动的。 [8]

那些宣布裁员并越来越多地将人工智能作为驱动因素的公司又如何呢？[9]行业领袖和劳工经济学家都对这些说法表示了一些合理的怀疑。[10]虽然一些小规模裁员可能与人工智能相关的自动化有关，但其他裁员似乎是出于为人工智能投资释放现金流或在大流行时代过度招聘后减少员工数量的愿望。 人力资源主管表示，人工智能的影响在角色整合和避免招聘人工智能可以自动化许多任务的角色方面更加明显。 [11]

这并不意味着人工智能不会对某些工人产生任何负面影响；相反，迄今为止的影响比迫在眉睫的“人工智能就业启示录”所暗示的更为微妙。 人工智能可能会造成一些在总体经济数据中不易察觉的破坏。 特别是，有一些证据表明人工智能可能会对年轻白领的需求产生负面影响，正如我们接下来讨论的那样。

年轻工人面临的艰难劳动力市场可能部分归因于人工智能

应届毕业生正面临多年来最具挑战性的就业市场，2026 年初应届毕业生失业率达到 5.6%，比三年前上升 1.6 个百分点。 [12]这种增长引发了人们的担忧，即人工智能正在取代许多应届毕业生曾经寻求的工作。 初级职位通常涉及日常研究、分析和写作任务，这些任务现在很大程度上可以通过人工智能来完成。 与这种直觉相一致的是，经验证据表明人工智能可能会抑制对新员工的需求。

在一篇广泛讨论的论文中，Brynjolfsson、Chandar 和 Chen 报告称，自 2022 年 ChatGPT 推出以来，从事人工智能职业的早期职业工人的就业率显着下降，尤其是软件开发人员和客户服务代表。 相比之下，如图 2 所示，从事相同职业的老年工人的就业保持相对稳定或持续增长。 作者将这些年轻工人比作“煤矿里的金丝雀”，他们是第一个经历人工智能对劳动力市场破坏的人。 [13]此后，其他研究人员也发现，从 2022 年开始，美国和英国雇用接触人工智能的年轻工人也会产生类似的负面影响。 [14]

图 2：2021-2026 年两种人工智能相关职业按年龄划分的就业情况

(a) 客户服务代表
(b) 软件开发商

这种影响的时机有些令人惊讶。 2022 年，人工智能模型的能力非常有限。 其他因素可能也在发挥作用，包括利率上升、疫情期间的过度招聘和远程工作。 例如，为了应对不断上升的通胀，美联储从 2022 年 3 月开始大幅加息——距离 ChatGPT 于次年 11 月公开发布还有几个月。 两篇新论文发现，在美联储货币政策转变之后、ChatGPT 首次亮相之前，人工智能相关职业的招聘开始下降。 [15]此外，疫情期间迅速转向远程工作可能会减慢在职学习速度，从而削弱了雇用年轻员工的价值。 新的证据表明，大流行之后，远程友好型职业的招聘开始倾向于更有经验的员工。 [16]

为了回应对这些和其他可能的混杂效应的担忧，布林约尔松和合著者添加了新的控制措施。 在这些结果中，入门级工人的就业下降直到 2024 年才显着。[17]因此，人工智能以外的其他因素似乎有可能导致 2022 年左右年轻工人的雇佣下降。 然而，到 2024 年，人工智能的采用和模型能力都取得了显着进步，使得人工智能的直接影响更加可信。

2022 年左右，人工智能相关职业的初级员工招聘明显下降。 更难确定的是，这种下降是否构成人工智能对现在或未来年轻工人需求影响的明确证据。 考虑到此时劳动力需求面临的其他宏观经济冲击，从经验上隔离人工智能的影响具有挑战性。 这仍然是一个开放且活跃的研究领域。

人工智能对员工生产力的影响有好有坏，但总体来说是积极的。

在实验环境中，人们经常发现生成式人工智能工具（例如聊天机器人和编码工具）可以极大地提高经验不足和绩效较差的员工的绩效。 在一项此类研究中，研究人员分析了生成式人工智能助手对大型呼叫中心客户支持代理的影响。 [18]该助手将整体生产力提高了 15%，其中收益主要集中在新手和低技能工人身上，他们每小时解决的问题数量增加了 30%。 高技能客服人员的绩效没有提高，其响应质量略有下降。

其他研究还表明，人工智能工具通常会加快任务完成速度，尽管效果因任务、环境和技能水平而异。 图 3 总结了人工智能工具对各种任务速度影响的研究结果。 在软件开发中，使用 GitHub Copilot（一种建议代码和函数的 AI 工具）可以使任务完成速度提高 56%，收益主要集中在经验较少的程序员身上。[19]在另一篇论文中发现了对软件开发的更温和的影响，影响范围从 10% 到 30%，具体取决于部署它的公司。 [20]在写作任务中，发现使用 ChatGPT 可以减少各种能力的工作者的写作时间，并提高低能力作家的写作质量。 [21]在年轻律师中，使用人工智能工具可以提高法律工作的速度，例如起草合同。 [22]在医疗环境中，对人工智能抄写员的评估发现了一些证据表明它们提高了医疗笔记的速度，尽管效果很小并且偶尔的不准确需要医生的监督。 [23]

图 3：生成式 AI 对任务速度影响的实验估计

在许多工作场所环境中，员工必须确定何时以及如何部署人工智能辅助，这使事情变得相当复杂。 Dell’Acqua 和合著者记录道，人工智能的功能是“参差不齐的”，这意味着性能可能会非常积极或消极，具体取决于其部署的具体任务。 [24]确定人工智能输出是否有用或需要进一步完善可能需要熟练的判断。 例如，当研究人员部署人工智能助手来帮助肯尼亚企业家时，技能较低的企业家使用人工智能工具获得的收入和利润低于那些不使用人工智能工具来发展业务的企业家。 [25]在研究原因时，研究人员发现，技能较差的企业家更有可能根据人工智能工具的一般建议采取行动，而这对他们的具体情况不利，而表现较好的企业家则提取更适合其业务需求的建议。

虽然人工智能可以提高一些员工的个人生产力，但它也会缩小创意的范围。 人们发现，在创意写作任务中使用人工智能可以提高技能较差的作家创作的故事的质量，但人工智能生成的故事比人类生成的故事更相似。 [26]郝和合著者发现，虽然采用人工智能工具的科学家发表了更多论文，但人工智能的采用减少了研究主题的总数以及科学家之间的互动。 [27]

人工智能显然有潜力在许多环境中提高员工的绩效。 然而，一些摩擦可能会阻止实验研究中观察到的成果在总体生产率指标中体现出来。 相对于经济任务的总数，人工智能可以有利地加速的任务份额可能很小。 [28]人工智能目前无法提供帮助的流程中的瓶颈可能会暂时限制生产力的提高。 [29]此外，当企业采用新技术时，衡量的生产率最初可能会下降，因为企业需要转移资源来重组职能并进行补充投资。 [30]虽然人工智能最终可能会提高生产力，但考虑到目前企业采用的速度，它可能在总体统计数据中还无法显现出来。

企业的采用速度有所加快，但在整个经济中并不均衡。

如果人工智能确实是一项变革性技术，那么无论其产生的全面影响是三年还是二十年，都会从根本上改变政策问题。 快速的转型可能会立即取代许多工人，而较慢的转型则可以给政策制定者和工人更多的时间来适应。 人工智能对整个经济产生潜在影响的时间和分布的最重要指标之一是企业采用的速度。

图 4：2023-2026 年人工智能在工作中的采用

对企业的调查显示，采用率存在很大差异，但都显示人工智能的使用在快速增长。 图 4 显示了几种被广泛引用的企业采用指标。 对企业采用率最保守的估计是人口普查局的商业趋势和前景调查 (BTOS)，这是一项全国范围内具有代表性的企业调查，目前估计约有 20% 的企业使用人工智能。 工作场所人工智能使用的其他衡量标准通常显示公司采用率较高；在高端，一项针对美国公司高管的调查发现，超过 80% 的员工在工作中使用人工智能。 [31]金融科技费用管理公司 Ramp 估计，超过 50% 的客户在人工智能工具和人工智能供应商上花钱。 一项全国范围内的家庭代表性调查发现，超过 40% 的就业受访者在工作中使用人工智能。

不同指标采用率的差异很大程度上是由于方法和样本构成的差异造成的。 较大的公司更有可能采用人工智能，因此就业加权采用率高于简单的公司计数所显示的水平。 Ramp 在其人工智能指数的方法中明确指出，使用其平台的公司并不是具有代表性的企业样本，并且偏向人工智能采用率较高的科技公司。 在对人工智能采用率调查的回顾中，美联储最近的一份研究报告指出了支持相对较低的人口普查估计值的充分理由，该估计值使用了全国抽样框架，并显示了当每项调查都按就业加权时，不同调查的采用率差异如何大幅缩小。 [32]

采用人工智能的公司分布告诉我们人工智能的影响可能首先发生在哪里。 目前，调查证据表明人工智能的采用集中在科技公司和金融等信息密集型行业。 最常见的人工智能部署是在销售和营销、IT、战略、财务和会计领域。 即使在采用者中，人工智能的使用仍然狭窄而不是广泛，仅限于一两个业务功能或在更广泛的任务中低频使用，全面的人工智能集成是例外而不是规则。 [33]麦肯锡最近的一项调查发现，大多数企业仍处于人工智能的实验和试点阶段，只有少数大公司在试点以外的扩展方面处于领先地位。 [34]

人工智能的采用似乎对就业也没有产生什么影响。 在人口普查数据中，只有 5% 的公司报告了对就业的影响，报告收益和损失的公司数量相同。 亚特兰大联邦储备银行调查的 80% 的高管表示，人工智能投资尚未改变他们的员工数量或提高生产力。 丹麦的一项大规模研究将工人采用人工智能的数据与公司联系起来，发现人工智能的采用会导致工人任务和时间的重组，但这些变化尚未影响工人的就业、工作时间或收入。 [35]最近的一项研究发现，在采用人工智能的公司中，就业率在采用后的两年内增长了 10%。 [36]

总而言之，这些数据表明，企业人工智能的采用正在迅速发展，但在整个经济中并不均衡，许多企业仍处于实验阶段，只有更先进的采用者才能更广泛地部署人工智能。

结论：现有证据并不是最后的结论。

技术进步通常需要数年甚至数十年的时间才能改变企业和劳动力市场。 1987 年，经济学家罗伯特·索洛 (Robert Solow) 曾说过一句著名的俏皮话：“你随处都可以看到计算机时代，但唯独生产力统计数据除外。” 创新与增长之间出现这种滞后是因为企业对新技术的采用往往不均衡且缓慢。 例如，企业在 20 世纪 80 年代对 PC 技术进行了大量投资。 但利用个人电脑的优势需要额外的投资——企业软件、员工再培训和组织重组。 这些采用摩擦是计算机革命直到 20 世纪 90 年代末才出现可衡量的经济回报的主要原因。

预测接下来会发生什么总是很难的。 在硅谷，一些人认为人工智能是一种“正常技术”（具有变革性但渐进性，类似于过去的技术），而另一些人则预测最早在 2027 年就会产生改变世界的影响。 人工智能作为一种普通技术的最有力的理由是历史。 以前的技术革命消除或减少了某些职业的劳动力需求，同时创造了新的就业机会和产业。 结果，即使工作性质和经济发生了变化，总就业人数仍然增加。

相比之下，那些认为人工智能有根本不同的人指出人工智能采用的速度异常快、人工智能对认知工作的影响不成比例，以及人工智能的跨领域性质，不仅威胁到一种职业，还威胁到许多白领工作。 无论哪个阵营是正确的，技术革命都可能对个人产生深刻的颠覆性影响，因此尽快更好地了解人工智能对劳动力市场不断变化的影响并准备潜在的政策应对措施至关重要。
